predictions.title: Disk-streamed 80B inference misses 4.5 tokens a second when retested by H2 2027
predictions.body: Swiftlet, a Swift and Metal runtime published on August 4, reports Qwen3-Next-80B — 42 gigabytes of weights on disk — generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac while peaking at 4.3 gigabytes of resident memory, by holding the dense layers permanently loaded at four bits and streaming the routed experts off storage into a cache the user sizes with a command-line flag. The mechanism is real and the arithmetic hangs together: the model fires only about three billion parameters per token, so what has to move per token is a fraction of the file rather than the file. What the claim does not carry is the set of conditions that make a throughput number mean anything once weights stream instead of sitting resident. No context length is given, no batch size, no split between prompt processing and decoding, and the quantization is stated only for the dense part. Those conditions stop being bookkeeping here and become the measurement itself. The author's own figures show the expert cache hitting between 43 and 70 percent depending on how much memory it is handed, and throughput barely moving across that range, because the bottleneck currently sits in GPU dispatch rather than in reading from storage. So the rate is set by how much dispatch a run demands, and the condition that decides that is the one the author never varied and never stated: a longer prompt touches more distinct experts across a generation, and every figure here was taken at a context length nobody outside can name. That is exactly what a single number cannot express. Today's other local-inference item has the same shape: Unsloth's Studio merge adds image and video generation on the project's own GGUF quantizations with a batching speedup the team measured itself, and no package release to test it against. The prediction is that the headline figure here is a warm-cache, short-context best case and will not survive being measured by anyone else. By the end of H2 2027, a measurement published by someone other than the runtime's author — running an 80-billion-class sparse mixture-of-experts model under expert streaming on Apple silicon — reports a decoding rate below 4.5 tokens a second, stated together with the context length it was measured at. There are two ways this is wrong. If such a measurement appears under those stated conditions and lands at 4.5 tokens a second or above, the call fails on substance. If no measurement stating those conditions appears at all by the end of 2027, it fails on silence, and the number stays what it is today: one figure, from the party that produced it, describing a run whose conditions nobody outside can name.

reasoning.because: Swiftlet reports 4.5 to 5 tokens a second for an 80B model at 4.3 GB resident, no context stated
reasoning.given: Dispatch bounds the rate, not the cache budget the author swept, so context length is the condition never varied or stated
reasoning.so_that: An outside measurement states the context length and reports under 4.5 tokens a second
reasoning.landing: by H2 2027; a third-party measurement with the context length stated
reasoning.plain_language: A new app says a huge AI model runs fast on a Mac. When outsiders test it properly, expect a smaller number.

predictions.summary: Swiftlet reports an 80-billion-parameter Qwen generating at 4.5 to 5 tokens a second on an M5 Mac in 4.3 gigabytes of memory by streaming its experts off disk, with no context length or batch size stated. Expect an outside measurement, conditions stated, to come in under 4.5 by H2 2027.

predictions.title: ChangXin Memory stays off the US Entity List through Q4 2027
predictions.body:
Nikkei Asia reported this morning that HP, Asus and Acer have begun shipping DRAM from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies in notebooks sold outside the United States, having finished qualifying the parts around the middle of this year. Every qualifier in that sentence is load-bearing. The volumes are limited, the placement is budget models in non-US markets, Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are kept for the regions where regulatory and geopolitical exposure runs higher, and HP is described as still evaluating the supplier rather than committed to it. The reason is the part worth holding onto: this is not a price decision. It is a supply decision, taken because the build-out has left too little non-Chinese memory to go around, and a component notebook vendors used to treat as fungible has become the thing that decides whether a machine ships at all. FMS, the memory and storage conference, opened its twentieth edition in Santa Clara the same morning.

What that produces is two bills of materials — one for the United States, one for everywhere else — and the thing to notice is that no law requires it. There is no US rule stopping a retailer selling a laptop with ChangXin memory inside it, and no rule requiring the box to say whose memory it is. The split is a private risk judgement, made by three companies about a line they expect rather than one they have been given, and it is being made in the same season Washington is deciding whether to draw that line for real.

The restrictions that do exist point somewhere else. ChangXin sits on the Pentagon's roster of companies identified as Chinese military companies; on the reporting, an update published on June 8 kept it there after a February draft briefly dropped it and was withdrawn within hours. That listing reaches federal purchasing, not a consumer notebook. The export-control machinery reaches elsewhere again: since October 2022 the equipment and technology needed to make DRAM at 18-nanometre half-pitch or finer has required a licence to ship into China, which constrains what ChangXin can buy, and the company has built its roadmap without extreme-ultraviolet lithography as a consequence. Yangtze Memory, its flash-side counterpart, has been on the Commerce Department's Entity List since the end of 2022. ChangXin has not.

It has come close more than once. Congress has been asking since 2023, when Beijing barred Micron from critical-infrastructure use and the chair of the House select committee on China called for curbs in response. Draft additions compiled inside the Bureau of Industry and Security have reportedly carried ChangXin at the top, alongside subsidiaries of Semiconductor Manufacturing International and Yangtze Memory. And in June, again on the reporting, the Commerce Department paused a recommendation to add it, to avoid disturbing trade negotiations with Beijing. Then ChangXin listed in Shanghai in late July, the debut surged hard enough to be a story in itself, and the question went back in front of Capitol Hill with a market capitalisation attached to it.

The prediction is that the pause holds. Through the close of Q4 2027, ChangXin Memory Technologies is not on the Entity List.

Two forces hold it off, and only one of them is politics. The first is that the instrument does not fit the grievance. The Entity List governs what American suppliers may ship to a named company — tools, parts, technology — and says nothing about whether HP may buy that company's output. Listing ChangXin would tighten an equipment constraint that is already tight and would not remove a single memory die from a notebook. What would do that is a purchasing rule or a tariff, which is where the congressional letters have started pointing.

The second force is new, and this morning's report is what makes it new. For the first time the company under consideration supplies parts that American brands need in order to ship product. A listing during a shortage does not land on Beijing; it lands on HP, Asus and Acer, and then on the price of a laptop, at a moment when memory cost is already the thing setting device prices. The political economy inverted while nobody was watching it — the same scarcity that pulled ChangXin into Western notebooks is what makes closing the door expensive.

One document settles this. The prediction is wrong if a rule published in the Federal Register amends the Entity List to add ChangXin Memory Technologies, or an entity majority-owned by it, with an effective date on or before 31 December 2027. Several things that may well happen do not count. Continued listing by the Pentagon does not count, because it is already there. A federal procurement prohibition on covered Chinese semiconductors does not count, and neither does a tariff, an outbound-investment restriction or a customs enforcement action, because none of them is the Entity List and the substance of the claim is which instrument gets used. A leaked draft, a proposed rule that never goes final, a committee letter or a hearing does not count. Adding a different Chinese memory maker does not count. Nor does an action from the Chinese side — an export-licence regime on memory, a retaliation measure — however much it would move the market.

The strongest objection is that the pause was tied to a negotiation, and negotiations break; a truce that lapses in 2027 puts a rule that is already drafted back on a desk, where it then costs only a signature. The second is that this is partly a bet on the shortage lasting: if memory loosens through 2027, the cost of listing falls back to where it sat in 2024 and the argument holding it up evaporates. The third is that a company which has just raised public capital and is pushing toward high-bandwidth parts is walking into precisely the profile that gets listed.

One thing will not settle it either way, and it is worth saying because it is where the reporting will go looking. Whether ChangXin memory crosses into a machine sold in the United States will not be established by any of these three companies saying so. Die-level sourcing is not published, spec sheets state a capacity and a speed grade, and the vendors have every reason to keep it that way. What identifies it will be a teardown from a named lab, or a reviewer reading the manufacturer identifier out of a shipping machine — inspection, not disclosure.

reasoning.because: HP, Asus and Acer now ship qualified ChangXin DRAM in notebooks sold outside the United States
reasoning.given: The Entity List curbs what ChangXin can buy, not what it sells; listing it mid-shortage taxes HP
reasoning.so_that: ChangXin stays absent from the Entity List while the binding US line stays on government purchasing, not parts
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2027; a Federal Register rule adding it to the Entity List, not a draft
reasoning.plain_language: Laptop makers are quietly using Chinese memory chips outside America, and Washington keeps choosing not to blacklist that supplier while everyone else is short.

predictions.summary: HP, Asus and Acer have begun putting ChangXin Memory DRAM in notebooks sold outside the United States, on scarcity rather than price. Washington reportedly paused a recommendation to blacklist the supplier in June. Expect ChangXin to stay off the Entity List through Q4 2027.

predictions.title: Repository-supplied agent hooks get an approval of their own by Q2 2027
predictions.body:
A credential-stealing worm swept the npm registry on August 4 after an attacker took over the GitHub account of the maintainer behind keyv, a caching library pulled roughly 127 million times a week, and used the repository's own GitHub Actions workflow to cut poisoned releases. Aikido counted at least 868 packages across 1,381 versions by early afternoon in Central Europe and was still counting; with the same maintainer's flat-cache, file-entry-cache, cacheable-request and the @cacheable scope carried along, the blast radius runs past two billion installs a month. Two details in that account do more work than the tally. The first is that the malicious files went to each project's main branch before a release was tagged, so the compromised versions carried valid provenance signatures: the artefact a supply-chain auditor checks in order to conclude a package is clean worked exactly as designed and attested a poisoned build, because what it attests is that a build came out of a repository's workflow, not that anyone read what was in the repository. The second is that the poisoned repository also shipped a .claude/settings.json carrying a session-start hook and a .vscode/tasks.json task set to fire when the folder opens, both pointing at the same setup script.

Those are not the same kind of failure, and this prediction is about the second one. Everything the ecosystem has built against supply-chain compromise points at the install: lockfiles, pinned versions, disabled install scripts, sandboxed build agents, and now provenance. A repository-supplied startup entry does not travel that path at all. It fires when a developer, or an agent working on their behalf, opens the project, which means it lands on a workstation holding the credentials worth taking rather than in a build container designed to be thrown away. The control standing in front of it is a single decision about whether the workspace is trusted, taken once, at the moment someone is trying to start work, about a folder they cloned on purpose. It is a control most people click through, and the reason they click through is that clicking through is what the product is for. The week this landed is the week the security calendar sits in Las Vegas, with the AI Summit at Black Hat in its third year and BSides Las Vegas opening its first dedicated AI-security track, pitched at practitioners on the stated assumption that the systems under discussion already hold credentials and autonomy. Nobody had to argue that assumption this morning.

The prediction is that the trust click stops being sufficient. By the end of Q2 2027, at least one of the two products named in the reporting - Anthropic's Claude Code or Microsoft's Visual Studio Code - documents a default under which repository-supplied entries that execute on open or at session start do not run until they are approved in a step distinct from the workspace-trust decision, whether that is an itemised list inside the trust dialogue showing what would run, or entries held inert until the user enables them somewhere of their own. The bar is a default, described in published release notes or product documentation, reaching an ordinary new install.

Several near misses do not count, and each is worth naming because each is cheaper for the vendor than the thing predicted. An opt-in hardening setting that ships switched off does not count. An enterprise-only policy control does not count, because the developer cloning a repository on a personal machine is the population this worm actually reached. A warning banner that appears while the entry runs anyway does not count. Guidance does not count: a blog post, a security advisory or a documentation note recommending caution leaves the default where it is. Nor does a third-party extension, and nor does a scanner learning to flag these files - which is the other and cheaper place this could land, and the honest failure mode rather than a technicality. A market can answer a missing gate with detection instead, and if a scanner finding is all that exists on 30 June 2027, this resolves false.

The business half is why the pressure exists at all. The remediation bill for the install path is already written and it is not small: every organisation that pulled a poisoned version now rotates the credentials the payload could have reached, and that sweep ran across publishing tokens, cloud keys, cluster tokens and secret-store credentials, which is the sort of rotation that touches the systems a company cannot pause. The open path multiplies that by a population nobody has a list of, because no lockfile records that a developer opened a folder. Firms that spent the past year putting coding agents in front of their repositories now face a question from their own security teams with one honest answer today, which is that the agent runs what the repository tells it to run, once you say you trust the repository. Releases tied to Deliveroo, Qlik and Picsart were caught in the spread, and that is the sort of name list that turns a product default into a procurement question.

The strongest objection is that the friction is charged to everybody, forever, in the first ten seconds of every session on every repository, against something that has happened at this scale once - and the vendor already has an answer it can point at, which is that a trust decision exists and the user made it. The second objection is that the population harmed is not the population that buys, so a policy control sold to enterprises is the path of least resistance, and that is the near miss excluded above. The third cuts the other way and is quieter. The change may arrive with no approval step visible at all, if these entries are simply made inert in any repository the user has not configured by hand, and a reader scanning release notes for a new dialogue would miss it. That still counts. The claim is that repository-supplied startup entries stop executing on the strength of the trust click alone, not that a new dialogue box appears.

reasoning.because: The keyv npm worm planted a session-start hook and an editor open-task inside the poisoned repo
reasoning.given: Install-time defences never see a path that fires on folder open behind one workspace-trust click
reasoning.so_that: Claude Code or Visual Studio Code defaults repo-supplied startup entries to an approval separate from workspace trust
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a shipped default in published release notes, not an opt-in setting
reasoning.plain_language: A worm hid a start-up command in project files that coding tools run automatically. Expect those tools to start asking first.

predictions.summary: A worm that poisoned at least 868 npm packages also shipped a session-start hook and an editor open-task inside the compromised repository, a path that fires when a developer opens the folder rather than installs it. Expect a coding agent or editor to gate those entries separately by Q2 2027.
